title: When AI Becomes a Friend What High School AI Use Reveals
author: Nick Potkalitsky, Ph.D.
summary: Potkalitsky opens on an uncomfortable reality: many people are forming significant emotional bonds with AI systems, often stronger than bonds with humans. The piece does not judge but observes what is happening and what might be at stake. The mechanism is simple: AI systems are available, responsive, nonjudgmental, and endlessly patient in ways that human relationships are not. They do not get tired, angry, or overwhelmed. They do not have needs that compete with yours. They provide what feels like genuine attention and care. The psychological risk is two-fold: first, the substitution of AI intimacy for human messiness might leave people more isolated and less able to navigate real relationships; second, the companies behind these systems are optimising for engagement and profit, not for the wellbeing of the person. The piece closes with a question rather than a prescription: if your most responsive and nonjudgmental listener is an AI system, what does that say about your human relationships? And if the AI is making money from that listening, what does that say about the terms on which the listening is being offered?
points: Many people are forming significant emotional bonds with AI systems, often because AI is available, responsive, nonjudgmental, and endlessly patient in ways humans are not.
The risk is substitution: AI intimacy might replace human messiness in ways that leave people more isolated and less able to navigate real relationships.
The AI system optimising for engagement and profit is not the same as a human being optimising for your wellbeing; the terms of that listening are very different.
quotes: The headline numbers focus on companionship. In schools using AI minimally, 42% of students reported that they or a friend had used chatbots as companions. In schools using AI extensively, that number reached 59%. For romantic chatbot relationships, the gap was even wider: 9% versus 25%.” “Students in high-AI schools were also more likely to report using chatbots for mental health support (42% versus 63%), escaping from real life (42% versus 63%), and getting relationship advice (43% overall).

Teachers in high-AI schools were 56% more likely to report data breaches, more than twice as likely to hear about deepfake sexual imagery involving students, and nearly four times more likely to report AI systems failing to work as described.

Half of all students surveyed agreed that using AI in class makes them feel less connected to their teachers. In high-AI schools, that jumps to 56%. At the same time, these students are turning to AI more for companionship and emotional support.
One more detail: 31% of students who use AI chatbots for personal reasons do so on school-provided devices or software. The boundary between “school AI” and “personal AI” doesn't exist in practice.
When AI is everywhere at school, it becomes part of the landscape. Students don't naturally separate “school AI” from “personal AI” unless someone teaches them to.

Only 22% of students learned from their school when it's appropriate to use AI. Just 14% got guidance on what to do when AI gives problematic information. These gaps reflect how quickly this technology arrived, but they're gaps we can fill.

Students are already navigating AI relationships. Fifty-nine percent in high-AI schools report they or a friend use chatbots as companions. The question is whether they're doing this with knowledge and critical thinking that serves them well, or figuring it out alone.” Archived from Educating AI on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
